accroche: In 1958, fleeing a raid alongside an entire Balinese village changed the fieldwork of two young anthropologists.
contenu_vulgarise:
Bali, April 1958. Ten days after arriving in the village, the anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his wife Hildred attend their first cockfight, held in the central square. Cockfights are banned under Indonesian law, a legacy of Dutch colonial law that the national government maintains, seeing it as a backward form of gambling. The police burst in, armed. The crowd scatters, running. Geertz and his wife have a choice: take out their papers, invoke their status as protected foreign visitors, or flee with everyone else. They choose to flee.

## An Incident That Opens a Field Site

The next day, the whole village treats them as fellow villagers. The couple that had been politely ignored for ten days becomes, overnight, the target of affectionate teasing, which in Bali is a sign of belonging rather than rejection. This is the turn that Geertz recounts at the opening of “Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight,” published in 1972 in the journal Daedalus, before it became one of the most widely read texts in 20th-century anthropology.

The cockfight itself, once the field site was won, becomes the object of analysis. Geertz sees in it less a game than a text that the Balinese tell themselves about themselves: the bets, often out of proportion to what they could bring in, stage status, kinship, and rivalry between neighborhood groups far more than the money at stake. He borrows from the philosopher Jeremy Bentham the term “deep play,” play so deep that the stakes exceed any rational justification apart from what they signify.

## A Method, Not Just an Example

The Bali article is not the theory itself; it is its most frequently cited demonstration. The theory goes by another name, “thick description,” a term Geertz develops in a neighboring essay in the same collection, borrowed from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle, who in 1968 distinguished a “thin” description of surface behavior (an eye that blinks) from a “thick” description, which restores the intention and context that make it a wink rather than a nervous twitch. Applied to ethnography, Geertz's idea holds that an anthropologist never describes a raw fact, but always one already interpreted, first his own, then that of the culture he observes.

The article was republished in 2005 by Daedalus for the journal's fiftieth anniversary, a sign, for a discipline that produces few texts that endure across decades, that fleeing on one afternoon in 1958 ended up counting for more than any theoretical article written without it.

repere.texte: Published in 1972 in the journal Daedalus (vol. 101, no. 1), the article was republished in 2005 by the same journal for its fiftieth anniversary, a text still regarded as foundational a third of a century after it first appeared.
repere.source: Clifford Geertz, “Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight,” Daedalus, vol. 134, no. 4, 2005 (republication)

carte.punch: Fleeing a raid made him an anthropologist the village accepted.
carte.idee: In 1958 in Bali, Clifford Geertz flees a police raid on an illegal cockfight rather than invoke his status as a foreigner. This gesture of solidarity opens the field site that will yield “Deep Play,” a foundational text of modern ethnography.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Wikipedia, “Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight”
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Detailed summary of the article and of the police raid anecdote.

quiz.question: Why does Clifford Geertz choose to flee the police raid with the villagers rather than invoke his status as a foreigner?
choix: Because the police would have arrested him anyway despite his status
This improvised solidarity got him accepted by the village, opening his field site
Because he did not know that cockfights were banned by law
Because he himself wanted to bet on the fight before the police burst in
quiz.explication: It was neither a legal accident, nor ignorance of the ban, nor a personal bet: it was this gesture of solidarity, fleeing rather than claiming a protected status, that transformed Geertz's relationship with the village and made his fieldwork possible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: From which philosopher does Geertz borrow the expression “deep play”?
choix: Gilbert Ryle, to whom he also owes the notion of thick description
Jeremy Bentham, for play whose stakes exceed all reason
The Balinese language, where it designates the highest bets
The journal Daedalus, which had used it before him
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Geertz takes “deep play” from Jeremy Bentham: play so deep that the stakes exceed any rational justification apart from what they signify. It is from Gilbert Ryle that he borrows the other notion, thick description.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Geertz, what do the bets at cockfights stage?
choix: Status, kinship, and rivalry between neighborhood groups
A breeding competition among the island's best breeders
Real enrichment, the winnings far exceeding the stake
A religious rite meant to win the favor of the gods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Geertz sees in the cockfight a text that the Balinese tell about themselves: the bets, often out of proportion to what they could bring in, put status and neighborhood rivalries at stake far more than money.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is a thick description, in the sense Geertz takes from Gilbert Ryle?
choix: An account that multiplies numerical measurements of behavior
A description that sticks to surface behavior, nothing more
An account that restores the intention and context giving the gesture its meaning
A method that compares the same gesture across several neighboring cultures
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1968, Ryle distinguished the thin description of an eye that blinks from the thick description, which says whether it is a wink or a nervous twitch. For Geertz, the ethnographer never describes a raw fact, but one already interpreted.
